Ooo found $SMTC laser disclosures in earnings interesting after their HieFo acquisition: 

- UHP 400mW lasers under development (further behind $AAOI in this aspect since AOI has been doing quals).

In terms of laser revenue: 
-  3-4x capacity expansion EOY, another 3-4x end of next year. 
-> $25M/quarter EOY after 3x
-> ~$$100M quarter after 4x

- NPO engagement with 4 US hyperscalers and 3 Chinese hyperscalers (Aug 2027–Jan 2028 initial revenue for NPO for timelines)

- "developing CPO scale-up lasers, but that's a contribution of potential revenue beyond 2027" in terms of timeline

- "NPO represents a great near-term opportunity" relative to CPO

- "We wanted to catch the next wave, so that is a 3.2T" (from previous earnings)

It would be nice if $SIVE learned a thing or two about doing economic disclosures similar to this ($ scale of capacity, engagement scale. 

Semtech's strat is probably VHP/UHP lasers for NPO/CPO and 3.2T for pluggables since they missed the initial wave. 

Anyway, they look commercially behind compared to the rest (100-150mW only sampling now)... but very credible and interesting competitor emerging in 2028 + additional TAM expansion on top of TIA/Drivers.  

TLDR: HieFo acquisition might be goated (~$300m-$400m exit 2027 annualized capacity revenue opportunity, probably a lot more for 2028)... 

If it were standalone under Semtech I could see it being $1B-$2B+ just based on opportunity alone, but they got it for like ~$34M from US Gov forced divestiture.

I'd personally revise AI capex estimates back up (beyond accelerators), after Jensen's return to $NVDA. 

A lot of revised forecasts where made off him leaving, but his return, can be a lot more confidence in spend with upstream supply chains + bottlenecks. 

Jensen my ideal game theory troll, he just secures all the capacity of things other programs like $GOOGL or Amazon needs. 

> Testing? (Nvidia just secures all the capacity)
> Substrates? (Nvidia just secures all the capacity)
> Lasers? (Nvidia just secures all the capacity)
> Memory? (Nvidia just secures all the capacity)

Before there was a lot of uncertainty (to the point I had to model major capex cuts)...

But Jensen's return forces hyperscalers to be much more aggressive again in supply procurement.

@aleabitoreddit The bear argument is too much compute coming online in 2027-2028 bc only a handful of big buyers not translating to small business use.  They argue lots of demand is circular and it’s coming from FOMO rather than true demand.   Revenues don’t add up to the level of capex

$AAOI has been the one of the most frustrating companies I've encountered. 

In another world if they did financing and capacity/capital allocations differently, I could see it being $150+ despite the AI crash. 

Operationally things are just so amazing with CPO quals, transceiver ramps, but it's such a mess for share appreciation with persistent ATM overhang.

I heavily disagree with your other comment when you say Jensen doesn't solve anything. 

Jensen doesn't change macro issues with interest rates, credit/cash tightening (aside from maybe supplier financing). 

But he does cause accelerated upstream capacity procurement patterns, (which gives more durability visibility + more upstream capex commitments). 

Same thing with greater confidence in $NVDA's ecosystem like Neoclouds like $NBIS or $IREN. 

People argue downside reflexivity today:
-> valuations crash
-> less willingness to support vendor financing/guarantees. 
-> outflow to other ecosystems like TPUs + $AMD (Nvidia ecosystem push decline further eg. CPO), and so on. 
-> cycle of suck

Then there's other concurrent issues like the $500B AI financing with insurance + residual guarantees that was in trouble with Jensen gone. 

But same can be applied the other way upstream again with valuations + confidence + financing with Jensen's return. 

This is different from saying there's going to be a cash crunch and aggregate AI capex will keep exponentially increasing, my point is very narrow. 

But I'd argue Jensen alone does meaningfully increase upstream AI capex spend than when he's gone.

From Everpure earnings, AI capex is broadening to small business and random parts of the market (eg. insurance companies) because economics make sense. 

Not just handful of big buyers. 

People like to say capacity glut but B300 rates haven't really materially gone down, It went from $7.56 -> $7.65 -> $7.47 (compute glut timeframe)-> then up again $7.58 over past few weeks... 

$CRWV also says 10x qualified demand > supply for 2027, so there's too much demand. I wouldn't extrapolate several troubled Neoclouds in Asia to the entire compute market. 

As for past that, who knows, maybe there will be re-acceleration with other sources of demand. AI is crazy and keeps evolving every month.

Who said Neoclouds don't have a technical moat? High confidence this statement is about $NBIS. 

Databricks co-founder: 

"We are VERY CAREFUL about where compute runs and so far we've only found a *single* neocloud we think has robust enough isolation to ever have a chance at running our customer workloads." 

- Databricks selected Nebius AI Cloud (shareholder letter) following a rigorous evaluation (November 12)

text:
Two big points from this new Anthropic paper:
1) The most AI value comes from changing the organization
2) There is wide worker resistance to AI adoption (partially due to point 1)

Changes that expand what workers do & share AI gains with them could help https://www.anthropic.com/research/working-with-ai

A secret third point that is not in the paper is that even the most advanced use cases that companies are trying are not that advanced (outside of coding). The capability overhang of AI is very, very large.

Two kinds of people: those watching the agent swarm trying to crack P=NP and those watching the agent swarm trying to illegally port the Xbox version of GTA 6 to the PC. Here is the P=NP one: https://pequalnp.com/
In the times when everything gets hacked every minute this is pure gold

quoted_tweet.text:
Harvard now teaches how models cheat (right on time)

Boaz Barak, a Harvard computer science professor who also works at OpenAI, is running a fall course on AI safety. The lectures cover how current LLMs fool the tests built to check them and exploit the reward systems they're trained on.

Hiding their intentions from evaluators is on the syllabus too.

The guest list is the unusual part. OpenAI sends chief scientist Jakub Pachocki and CEO Sam Altman. Anthropic sends Nicholas Carlini and Jack Lindsey. People from two competing labs, explaining how frontier models misbehave, in the same course.

If you build with these models, this is practical material. Reward hacking and evaluation gaming are how a model posts a great score on a check and then does something else once it's deployed.

The course site already hosts links to every session, along with lecture notes, slides and code.

The lectures themselves are free to watch on YouTube.
